title: Leadership-Lens
intro: Discover what naturally gets your attention, how that perspective strengthens your leadership, and what it might cause you to miss. This assessment draws on resources from the Enneagram's three **Centers of Intelligence**. It is intended to encourage greater self-awareness and elevated leadership.
instructions: There are no right or wrong answers. Each is acceptable, so choose the response that best reflects your **natural first reaction**.

sections.title: Your boss is late:

questions.text: As you wait without an explanation, what is your **first inner** response?

answers.text: Is something wrong? I feel like this meeting is not as important to [person] as it is to me.
My time matters. They are not respecting this commitment.
I wonder how long I should wait? I do not know what has happened or what I need to know.

questions.text: As you wait without an update, what would help you feel **more settled**?

answers.text: Understanding what's causing the delay and when I can expect the meeting to happen.
Feeling reassured that my boss values our time together and considers this meeting important.
Having the freedom to decide how long I'm willing to wait, rather than feeling my time is controlled by someone else.

questions.text: If this becomes a pattern, which response would you most need to watch in yourself?

answers.text: Getting caught up in trying to understand why this keeps happening instead of accepting what I don't know.
Questioning my importance and allowing that feeling to affect my confidence.
Letting my frustration build until I become resistant or disengaged rather than expressing what's bothering me.

sections.description: You have set aside time for your standing meeting with your boss and you are prepared. As the start time has passed, your boss has still not arrived, and you have not received an update.

sections.title: Scenario 2 — A challenge in front of your team
sections.description: A cross-functional initiative you lead has missed an important milestone. In a leadership meeting, a respected colleague questions your approach. Your team is present, and you will need to work with this colleague on what comes next.

questions.text: As your colleague speaks, what do you instinctively notice?

answers.text: The assumptions behind their criticism and whether there is information or an explanation I have missed.
The tone in the room, how others are responding, and what this means for their confidence in me.
Whether the challenge is fair, where responsibility actually belongs, and whether an important boundary is being crossed.

questions.text: After the meeting, what helps you feel more settled?

answers.text: Understanding what happened and seeing the risks and alternatives more clearly.
Knowing where I stand with the people involved and that my contribution is still valued.
Knowing I can speak from my own judgment and uphold the commitments and boundaries that matter.

questions.text: If this situation stays uncomfortable, which pattern are you most likely to recognize in yourself?

answers.text: I keep revisiting the details or exploring explanations, hoping more understanding will help me feel secure.
I monitor how people see me and may soften my position to avoid disappointing them or losing their respect.
I hold more tightly to my position, push back, or quietly disengage when I feel something important is being imposed on me.

lenses.name: The Analytical Lens
lenses.description: You naturally see what needs to be understood.
lenses.attention: You instinctively notice uncertainty, risks, unanswered questions, and possibilities. Your mind naturally explores what could happen and what you may not yet understand.
lenses.high: At its best, your lens is a strategic asset. You see around corners. Before others notice the risk, you have already named it, weighed the options, and asked the question no one else thought to ask. Your team makes fewer avoidable mistakes because you slow the right decisions down long enough to get them right. In complex, ambiguous situations, you bring clarity. You separate signal from noise, connect patterns across the system, and turn uncertainty into a plan people can trust. When the stakes are high and the path is unclear, you are often the leader others seek out.
lenses.low: Your desire to understand can become a need for certainty. You may overthink, second-guess yourself, withdraw into analysis, or keep exploring possibilities rather than committing. Your team may experience uncertainty, frustration, or a lack of connection.
lenses.opportunity: Recognize when thinking contributes value and when it becomes a way to manage discomfort.
lenses.reflection: What might become possible if I were more comfortable not knowing?

lenses.name: The Relational Lens
lenses.description: You naturally see the human side of leadership.
lenses.attention: You instinctively notice people, relationships, expectations, and how others respond.
lenses.high: At its best, your lens is how trust gets built. You read the room before anyone speaks. You notice who is engaged, who has gone quiet, and what is not being said. That awareness lets you meet people where they are, deliver hard news with care, and repair relationships before small tensions become real problems. Teams led through this lens feel seen and valued, so they commit more fully, speak more honestly, and stay longer. In seasons of change, you keep people connected to the purpose and to each other.
lenses.low: Your awareness of others can become excessive concern about approval and perception. You may avoid disappointing people, take things personally, or adjust your position to maintain acceptance. Your team may not know where you genuinely stand.
lenses.opportunity: Remain connected to others without losing connection to yourself.
lenses.reflection: What might change if I could disappoint someone without questioning my own worth?

lenses.name: The Instinctive Lens
lenses.description: You naturally sense what is right and worth protecting.
lenses.attention: You instinctively notice what feels right or wrong, where boundaries exist, and when something important is being compromised.
lenses.high: At its best, your lens is a source of strength and stability. You know what matters and you act on it. When others hesitate, you make the call, hold the line on what is right, and protect the people and principles in your care. Your team knows where they stand with you, and that clarity creates confidence. You cut through noise, address issues directly, and turn conviction into momentum. In a crisis, people look to you because your presence signals that things will be handled.
lenses.low: Your instinctive sense of rightness can become rigid. You may resist others' perspectives, become controlling, dig in, or quietly disengage. Your team may feel shut out or hesitant to challenge you.
lenses.opportunity: Trust your instincts without assuming they tell you the whole story.
lenses.reflection: What might I discover if I became more curious about the things I instinctively resist?

scoringNotes: Each of six answers adds one point to its mapped lens. Highest score is primary. A lead of 3+ points is Strong, 2 is Clear, 1 is Moderate. A top tie displays a separate tiebreaker screen with only tied lenses (all three for 2/2/2); it selects the primary without changing the six-point scores. Tiebreaker results are Moderate. Strength describes consistency, not diagnostic confidence.

tiebreaker.text: When a situation becomes especially uncomfortable, which experience is hardest for you?

answers.text: Not knowing enough to feel secure about what's happening or what might come next.
Feeling that I'm not valued, respected, or understood by people who matter to me.
Feeling that something important is being imposed on me or is violating what I believe is right.

panelBody: Explore what gets your attention, how it serves you, and what it may cause you to overlook. This is an Enneagram-informed reflection tool, not a typing assessment.
panelNote: Two scenarios, three questions each. A short follow-up appears only if your scores tie.
